items.html:
Recommend first benchmarking this minimal policy in threads::product:

let threads = if m == 1 || n == 1 {
    1
} else {
    (work / SEQUENTIAL_PRODUCT).clamp(1, current_num_threads())
};

It reuses the existing 65,536-work threshold, leaves pool ownership unchanged, and gives 64³ products four workers and 64×128×64 products eight.

Source evidence:

  • threads.rs:219–240 currently sends every above-threshold product to the entire available budget.
  • faer-0.24.4/src/linalg/matmul/mod.rs:1401–1410 passes the requested count directly to its x86 backend.
  • private-gemm-x86-0.1.20/src/lib.rs:1266 uses a 24×4 complex AVX512 microkernel. Its job grouping at 813–824 means 64×64 output exposes only four compute jobs; 64×128 exposes eight.
  • That backend nonetheless recruits all requested workers at 871 and 1511.
  • spindle-0.2.6/src/lib.rs:214–216,279–280 respects a reduced cap inside the existing larger Rayon pool. No pool redesign is needed.

Pitfalls to benchmark:

  1. 128×128: the work rule allows 32 workers, while the backend exposes roughly 12 output jobs. This may justify a second measured adjustment.
  2. Deep skinny products: the backend processes depth in chunks of at most 512 (private-gemm-x86:1272), so total m*n*k overstates useful parallel work when k is large. Consider min(k,512) only if real workloads show a consequential problem.
  3. Preserve serial vectors: faer’s column-major parallel matvec splits and reduces the inner dimension (matmul/mod.rs:977–1029), changing bits with worker count.
  4. Cross-platform evidence: ARM/non-AVX x86 uses gemm-common, which has a separate threading threshold. Avoid encoding AVX512 tile geometry in treams.

Existing thread tests cover only budgets (1,2,3) (tests/bindings/test_thread_pool.py:30). Extend meaningful matrix/stack exact-bit verification to actual capped and uncapped budgets, including 4, 16 and 32. I made no edits and ran no builds or tests.

items.html:
No missed forward product shape or compiler regression found.

For cluster.solve() with N16,L3, the only direct product path is LocalMatrix::apply_into: sixteen 30×480×30 products. Their work is 432,000, so the work cap is six and a four-thread budget remains four. The remaining work is LU factorization/solve, whose scheduling is independent.

Comparing frozen stage6 against work-cap-inline, normalized assembly is identical for:

  • LocalMatrix::apply_into: 222 instructions.
  • InteractionFactor::factorize: 510.
  • Lu::new and its closure: 533 and 291.
  • private_gemm_x86::gemm and inner closure: 1,040 and 1,072.
  • All three product_into closure bodies: 77 each.

The product wrapper retains its original 0x98 stack frame; differences are the intended worker-cap and overflow branches. Thus preserving the old ≤4-thread policy cannot change this workload’s mathematical or scheduling branch. Code placement or runtime scheduling remains possible; the source does not justify another heuristic.

For bitwise behavior, x86 GEMM’s depth chunks remain fixed at 512 independently of worker count; workers partition output/packing rather than summing partial products. Conjugation and strides change operand access but not the scheduling reduction. The existing serial m==1 || n==1 guard remains necessary. This is source support, not a proof for every backend/shape; retain exact-bit tests for skinny, deep, adjoint products.

No files changed; no builds or tests run.
